questions.prompt: Rania tells her partner: "Why not record yourself reading aloud?" How does she say exactly the same thing with "What about…?"

options.text: What about recording yourself reading aloud?
What about you record yourself reading aloud?
What about to record yourself reading aloud?
What about record yourself reading aloud?

questions.explanation: After "What about" English puts a noun or a verb in -ing, so the same suggestion becomes "What about recording yourself reading aloud?" The classic mistake is "What about to record yourself reading aloud?", which keeps the to of the infinitive where the -ing form is needed. "What about record yourself reading aloud?" keeps the base verb that belongs after Why not, and "What about you record yourself reading aloud?" turns a short offer into a full sentence, which the structure taught here does not take.

questions.prompt: Bilel asks Rym: "Have you got enough time to revise at home?" Which short answer says yes and is correct English?

options.text: Yes, I have got.
Yes, I have.
Yes, I do.
Yes, I've.

questions.explanation: A short answer repeats the helper of the question and stops there, and a positive one is never contracted, so the reply is "Yes, I have." "Yes, I have got." carries on with the main verb instead of stopping at the helper, "Yes, I do." brings in a helper the question never used, and "Yes, I've." contracts a positive short answer, which English does not allow.

questions.prompt: Read this exchange between two classmates after an English lesson: "Ghada: How did you find today's lesson? · Skander: The topic was quite interesting, but I only understood a little. · Ghada: The reading passage was too long for me. My strong point is writing. I'm not very good at listening. · Skander: Same here. Why not listen to an English podcast twice a week? · Ghada: Good idea. You could send me the link every Friday. · Skander: If you bring your headphones, we will listen to one at break." Ghada names a strong point and a difficulty. Which pair is hers?

options.text: Strong point: listening · Difficulty: writing
Strong point: reading · Difficulty: listening
Strong point: writing · Difficulty: listening
Strong point: writing · Difficulty: reading

questions.explanation: Ghada says "My strong point is writing. I'm not very good at listening.", so the pair is "Strong point: writing · Difficulty: listening". "Strong point: listening · Difficulty: writing" turns her two sentences round. The two pairs that name reading are baited by "The reading passage was too long", which is a remark about one text, not a strong point and not a difficulty. Skander is the one who only understood a little; he is not the speaker here.

questions.prompt: Nourhene tells her partner: "My main difficulty is spelling. I know the words when I hear them, but I write them wrong." Which suggestion actually answers that difficulty?

options.text: Why not watch an English film every Sunday?
You should join the debate club at your school.
You could learn ten new words by heart every week.
What about copying each new word three times?

questions.explanation: Nourhene hears the words correctly but writes them wrong, so she needs writing practice, and the suggestion that gives it is "What about copying each new word three times?" — copying is the only one of the four that puts a pen in her hand. The classic mistake is to pick a suggestion that is well built but aims at another skill: "Why not watch an English film every Sunday?" trains listening, "You should join the debate club at your school." trains speaking, and "You could learn ten new words by heart every week." adds words to her stock without ever making her write one.

questions.prompt: Sarra read the same article and it suited her exactly: not one page more than she wanted, not one page fewer. Aymen wanted fewer pages. Which pair reports the two of them?

options.text: Sarra: the right length · Aymen: too long
Sarra: too long · Aymen: the right length
Sarra: the right length · Aymen: very long
Sarra: too short · Aymen: too long

questions.explanation: Sarra wanted no more pages and no fewer, which is the right length, and Aymen wanted fewer, which is too long, because too means more than I want. The pair that swaps the two turns Sarra into the unhappy reader; "Aymen: very long" only states a fact about the length and carries no complaint at all; and "Sarra: too short" says she wanted more pages, the opposite of what she says.

questions.prompt: Youssef decides now to stop skipping the listening tasks. Which sentence states his resolution correctly?

options.text: I don't will skip the listening tasks.
I will not skipping the listening tasks.
I won't skip the listening tasks.
I won't to skip the listening tasks.

questions.explanation: A resolution is will or won't followed by the base verb, with nothing in between, so Youssef writes "I won't skip the listening tasks." The classic mistake is "I don't will skip the listening tasks.", which negates will with do as if it were an ordinary verb. "I will not skipping the listening tasks." puts an -ing form after will not, and "I won't to skip the listening tasks." slips the to of the infinitive between the helper and the verb.
